warmup.q: List.of(1) and List.of(1, 2, 3) both return a List<Integer>. What do you expect getClass() to say for each?
options: Both are the same private class
Two different private classes, chosen by the factory from the number of elements
List itself, since List.of is defined on the interface
warmup.why: List.of is a static factory, so it can return any class it likes. In JDK 21 it returns List12 for one or two elements and ListN for more, both private. A constructor could never do that: new X() always gives you an X. And an interface can't be created at all, so List itself is impossible. The first section shows the JDK's factories choosing, with real output.

opening:
Walk into the town bakery and ask for "a loaf for sandwiches". You don't name a recipe, and you don't pick an oven. The baker hears what you need and decides: today it's the white tin loaf. Next door, the furniture maker takes orders for dining sets. Ask for one in oak, and the table and the chairs come from the same workshop, so they match.

Code makes objects all day, usually with new, which names the exact class every time. That's fine until the choice depends on something: the weight of a parcel, a setting, whether we're in a test. Then the new calls spread through the program, each one deciding on its own, and one day a parcel booked with one courier gets tracked with the other.

In the last lesson, a private constructor and one getInstance() decided how many objects exist. In this lesson, we'll let a factory decide which object you get: static factories with names, factory methods passed around as functions, factories that return a sealed result instead of throwing, and an abstract factory for a set that must match. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started at the bakery counter and the furniture maker's workshop. In code, the counter became a static factory with a name, and the baker's choice became a function passed in. The workshop became one interface that makes a matching booker and tracker, and the compiler checked every switch.

Now search your own code for default -> or else -> in a switch or when that creates objects. Each is a place where a new case slips through without a word. If the type is sealed or an enum, delete the branch and see what the compiler says.

Next, we'll meet objects with many optional parts. When a constructor needs ten arguments, how do you build one that anyone can read?

sections.h: Static factory methods: constructors with names
sections.html:
Start with the counter at the bakery. You say what you want, and the baker hands over something that fits. You never see the kitchen. A static factory method is that counter in code: a static method that returns an instance of its class, or of some class behind an interface. Effective Java, the best-known book of Java advice, opens with it (item 1: consider static factory methods instead of constructors). The JDK, the libraries that come with Java, is full of them: List.of, Duration.ofMinutes, Integer.valueOf, Thread.ofVirtual.

A constructor can do one thing: make a new object of exactly its own class. A static factory can do four things a constructor can't.

  1. It has a name. Duration.ofMinutes(2) and Duration.ofSeconds(2) both take a long. Two constructors with the same parameter types can't exist, and new Duration(2) would say nothing anyway.
  2. It can return an object it made earlier. Integer.valueOf(100) hands back the same cached object every time.
  3. It can return any subtype, chosen from the input. List.of(1) and List.of(1, 2, 3) return two different private classes. EnumSet.noneOf picks a set backed by a single long when the enum has 64 constants or fewer, and a bigger one otherwise.
  4. The class it returns doesn't have to exist when the factory is written. JDBC, in java.sql, is Java's standard way to talk to a database, and each database company ships its own driver. DriverManager.getConnection(url) returns a connection from whichever driver on the classpath (the list of places the JVM loads classes from) accepts the URL, and those drivers were written long after java.sql.

The warm-up was the third point. FactoriesInTheJdk, in the Try it, asks each factory what it handed back. On JDK 21 it printed:

List.of(1)            -> List12
List.of(1, 2, 3)      -> ListN
EnumSet of TimeUnit   -> RegularEnumSet (7 constants)
EnumSet of scripts    -> JumboEnumSet (164 constants)

Same method, different classes, and you can't write any of those class names in your own code. The factory is the only door.

The downsides are small. A class with only private constructors can't have subclasses, which pushes you toward composition (building a class out of other objects instead of extending one) and costs little. Factories are also harder to spot than constructors, so stick to the usual names: of, from, valueOf, parse, newX, create.

For the shop's own value types, make this the default. Picture a Price with a private constructor and two doors, Price.ofCents(450) and Price.parse("4.50"). With the constructor private, every Price in the program went through your checks. The compare block at the end of this lesson writes it out in both languages.

A constructor can only say new. A factory can say what you mean, and choose.

A static factory makes its choice inside its own class. The next step moves the choice out, away from the code that uses the object.

try.title: Watch the JDK's factories choose
steps: Read FactoriesInTheJdk. For each of the first four lines, predict the class name you'll see. The Kotlin twin adds three lines for Kotlin's own listOf.
Run it from the labs/ folder with the command below.
Type RegularEnumSet in your editor, as if you wanted to use it. Can you?

code.title: FactoriesInTheJdk.java
code.html: package workbench.patterns.l02; import java.time.Duration; import java.util.EnumSet; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; /** Static factories in the JDK pick the class for you. Predict each class name before you run this. */ public class FactoriesInTheJdk { public static void main(String[] args) { // the factory picks an implementation based on the input System.out.println("List.of(1) -> " + List.of(1).getClass().getSimpleName()); System.out.println("List.of(1, 2, 3) -> " + List.of(1, 2, 3).getClass().getSimpleName()); System.out.println("EnumSet of TimeUnit -> " + EnumSet.noneOf(TimeUnit.class).getClass().getSimpleName() + " (" + TimeUnit.values().length + " constants)"); System.out.println("EnumSet of scripts -> " + EnumSet.noneOf(Character.UnicodeScript.class).getClass().getSimpleName() + " (" + Character.UnicodeScript.values().length + " constants)"); // the factory can hand back a cached instance instead of a new one System.out.println("valueOf(100) twice -> same object? " + (Integer.valueOf(100) == Integer.valueOf(100))); System.out.println("Duration.ofSeconds(0) -> same as ZERO? " + (Duration.ofSeconds(0) == Duration.ZERO)); // and its name says what you get, which a constructor can't System.out.println("Duration.ofMinutes(2) -> " + Duration.ofMinutes(2)); } }

alt.title: FactoriesInTheJdk.kt
alt.html: package workbench.patterns.l02 import java.time.Duration import java.util.EnumSet import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit // The same JDK factories called from Kotlin, plus Kotlin's own. Predict each class name first. fun main() { // JDK static factories pick an implementation from the input println("List.of(1) -> " + java.util.List.of(1).javaClass.simpleName) println("List.of(1, 2, 3) -> " + java.util.List.of(1, 2, 3).javaClass.simpleName) println("EnumSet of TimeUnit -> " + EnumSet.noneOf(TimeUnit::class.java).javaClass.simpleName + " (" + TimeUnit.entries.size + " constants)") println("EnumSet of scripts -> " + EnumSet.noneOf(Character.UnicodeScript::class.java).javaClass.simpleName + " (" + Character.UnicodeScript.entries.size + " constants)") // Kotlin's factory functions do the same (full names, since two of these are nested classes) println("listOf() -> " + listOf<Int>().javaClass.name) println("listOf(1) -> " + listOf(1).javaClass.name) println("listOf(1, 2, 3) -> " + listOf(1, 2, 3).javaClass.name) // a factory can hand back a cached instance, and its name says what you get println("Currency EUR twice -> same object? " + (java.util.Currency.getInstance("EUR") === java.util.Currency.getInstance("EUR"))) println("Duration.ofMinutes(2) -> " + Duration.ofMinutes(2)) }

try.expect: List12 for one element and ListN for three. RegularEnumSet for TimeUnit (7 constants) and JumboEnumSet for Character.UnicodeScript (164 constants on JDK 21). Both same object? lines print true, because the factories handed back cached objects. None of these classes is public, so your editor won't let you name them: the factory is the only door. Kotlin's listOf plays the same game, returning EmptyList, Collections$SingletonList or Arrays$ArrayList depending on how many elements you pass.

sections.h: Factory Method: let someone else choose the class
sections.html:
Here's the problem in the shop. When an order leaves, the shop tells the customer, by text message (SMS) or by email. Tests use a fake messenger that sends nothing. The code that writes the notice shouldn't decide which messenger it gets, or every test run would text real customers.

The Factory Method from the Gang of Four (GoF) book on design patterns is the classic answer. A class needs to create something, but it doesn't pick the concrete class. In the book's version, an abstract class declares a creation hook, the factory method, and subclasses override it:

Java
abstract class OrderNotices {
    protected abstract Messenger createMessenger();          // the factory method
    final String orderLeft(String customer) {
        return createMessenger().send(customer, "your order is on its way");
    }
}
class SmsNotices extends OrderNotices {
    protected Messenger createMessenger() { return new SmsMessenger(); }
}
Kotlin
abstract class OrderNotices {
    protected abstract fun createMessenger(): Messenger        // the factory method
    fun orderLeft(customer: String) = createMessenger().send(customer, "your order is on its way")
}
class SmsNotices : OrderNotices() {
    override fun createMessenger(): Messenger = SmsMessenger()
}

That works, and it's still a fair design when the subclass has other reasons to exist. But here it costs one subclass per product, just to pick a constructor. Since Java 8, a function does the same job. A Supplier<Messenger> (in Kotlin, a () -> Messenger) is a factory: call it, and you get a messenger. A constructor reference such as FakeMessenger::new, read as "call this constructor", is the shortest way to write one:

Java
record OrderNotices(Supplier<? extends Messenger> messengers) {
    String orderLeft(String customer) {
        return messengers.get().send(customer, "your order is on its way");
    }
}
new OrderNotices(SmsMessenger::new);    // the real program
new OrderNotices(FakeMessenger::new);   // a test
Kotlin
class OrderNotices(private val messengers: () -> Messenger) {
    fun orderLeft(customer: String) = messengers().send(customer, "your order is on its way")
}
OrderNotices(::SmsMessenger)    // the real program
OrderNotices(::FakeMessenger)   // a test

That's the bakery counter in code: OrderNotices asks for "a messenger" and never names a class. The real program and the test each hand in their own way to make one.

When the choice depends on data, such as a setting or the customer's preference, put it in one static factory over a sealed family. A sealed interface lists every class that may implement it, so the compiler knows them all:

Java
static Messenger of(Channel c) {
    return switch (c) {            // no default branch, on purpose
        case SMS -> new SmsMessenger();
        case EMAIL -> new EmailMessenger();
        case FAKE -> new FakeMessenger();
    };
}
Kotlin
fun messengerOf(c: Channel): Messenger = when (c) {   // no else branch, on purpose
    Channel.SMS -> SmsMessenger()
    Channel.EMAIL -> EmailMessenger()
    Channel.FAKE -> FakeMessenger()
}

Leave out default (else in Kotlin). Say the shop, in a burst of nostalgia, adds PIGEON to the enum. The switch stops compiling, and the compiler points at the one place that needs a new messenger:

MessengerFactory.java:14: error: the switch expression does not cover all possible input values

The compiler is a strict foreman here: it won't build the program until every case has a product. Now add a catch-all branch that returns FakeMessenger, and the build stays green while every pigeon notice goes to the fake. Nothing warns you. That's where the bakery picture breaks. A baker improvises when you ask for something new, and a factory with a default branch improvises too, badly.

A factory's switch gets no default. Let the compiler find the new case.

People mix up the two names, so let's keep them apart. A static factory is about how one class hands out its own instances. Factory Method is about who decides the concrete class: not the code that uses the object.

Kotlin has no static keyword at all, though. So where do its factories live?

try.title: Break a factory on purpose
steps: Add PIGEON to the Channel enum and run it again. Read the compiler error.
Now add a catch-all as the last branch (default -> new FakeMessenger(); in Java, else -> FakeMessenger() in Kotlin), keep PIGEON, and run again. Where does the pigeon notice go?

code.title: MessengerFactory.java
code.html: package workbench.patterns.l02; import java.util.function.Supplier; /** A factory method over a sealed family, and the same factory passed around as a function. */ public class MessengerFactory { enum Channel { SMS, EMAIL, FAKE } sealed interface Messenger permits SmsMessenger, EmailMessenger, FakeMessenger { String send(String to, String text); // the static factory: an exhaustive switch over the enum, with no default branch static Messenger of(Channel c) { return switch (c) { case SMS -> new SmsMessenger(); case EMAIL -> new EmailMessenger(); case FAKE -> new FakeMessenger(); }; } } record SmsMessenger() implements Messenger { public String send(String to, String text) { return "sms to " + to + ": " + text; } } record EmailMessenger() implements Messenger { public String send(String to, String text) { return "email to " + to + ": " + text; } } record FakeMessenger() implements Messenger { public String send(String to, String text) { return "fake: nothing sent"; } } // the modern "factory method": the caller hands in how to make the product record OrderNotices(Supplier<? extends Messenger> messengers) { String orderLeft(String customer) { return messengers.get().send(customer, "your order is on its way"); } } public static void main(String[] args) { for (Channel c : Channel.values()) { System.out.println(c + " -> " + Messenger.of(c).send("anna", "your order is on its way")); } System.out.println("test notices -> " + new OrderNotices(FakeMessenger::new).orderLeft("anna")); } }

alt.title: MessengerFactory.kt
alt.html: package workbench.patterns.l02 // A factory over a sealed family, and the same factory passed around as a function. enum class Channel { SMS, EMAIL, FAKE } sealed interface Messenger { fun send(to: String, text: String): String companion object { // the factory: an exhaustive when over the enum, with no else branch fun of(c: Channel): Messenger = when (c) { Channel.SMS -> SmsMessenger() Channel.EMAIL -> EmailMessenger() Channel.FAKE -> FakeMessenger() } } } class SmsMessenger : Messenger { override fun send(to: String, text: String) = "sms to $to: $text" } class EmailMessenger : Messenger { override fun send(to: String, text: String) = "email to $to: $text" } class FakeMessenger : Messenger { override fun send(to: String, text: String) = "fake: nothing sent" } // the modern "factory method": the caller hands in how to make the product class OrderNotices(private val messengers: () -> Messenger) { fun orderLeft(customer: String) = messengers().send(customer, "your order is on its way") } fun main() { for (c in Channel.entries) { println("$c -> ${Messenger.of(c).send("anna", "your order is on its way")}") } println("test notices -> ${OrderNotices(::FakeMessenger).orderLeft("anna")}") }

try.expect: The first run prints one line per channel, then test notices -> fake: nothing sent. With PIGEON added, the build fails at the factory: javac says error: the switch expression does not cover all possible input values, and kotlinc says 'when' expression must be exhaustive. Add the 'PIGEON' branch or an 'else' branch. With a catch-all branch it compiles and prints PIGEON -> fake: nothing sent. A real customer's notice would go to the fake, and nothing warns you.

aside.title: Does my framework write factory methods for me?
aside.html: If you write web services, it probably calls them. In Spring, a method marked @Bean builds an object; in Quarkus, a method marked @Produces does the same. The framework calls that method and passes the result to every class that asks for the interface, so the rest of the code never names the concrete class. The framework calls it when it creates the object, not once per request. A choice that depends on the current request, such as the weight of this parcel, still needs a factory you call yourself.

video.title: Checkout asks a factory for a gateway and never names the class; when an authorizer and a refunder must match, one call picks the whole card-network family

sections.h: Kotlin factories: companion objects, invoke and sealed results
sections.html:
Kotlin's factories live in three other places.

The companion object is the direct translation of a Java static factory: make the constructor private, and put the factory next to it. Here's the lab's Parcel. The shop sends light parcels with a bike courier and heavy ones by van, so a parcel knows its weight and which courier can carry it:

Java
public final class Parcel {
    private final Courier courier;
    private final int grams;
    private Parcel(Courier courier, int grams) { this.courier = courier; this.grams = grams; }

    public static ParcelResult parse(String raw) { /* check, then new Parcel(courier, grams) */ }
}
Kotlin
class Parcel private constructor(val courier: Courier, val grams: Int) {
    companion object {
        fun parse(raw: String): ParcelResult { /* check, then Parcel(courier, grams) */ }
    }
}

Parcel.parse("2.5 kg") both checks the text and picks the courier. That's the bakery again: you say the weight, and the factory decides who carries it.

An operator fun invoke on the companion lets callers write what looks like a constructor call, Fee(250). Behind it runs a factory that can check the value or return a cached one. invoke is the function Kotlin calls when you put parentheses after an object. Use it sparingly, because readers expect Fee(250) to make a new object.

The third shape is a top-level function named like the type. Kotlin's coding conventions allow a factory function to share the name of the abstract type it returns, and the kotlinx.coroutines library does exactly that: Job() and MutableStateFlow(0) are functions that return a private class.

What a factory returns matters as much as where it lives. A parser that throws makes every caller remember a try. A factory that returns a sealed result, a sealed set of possible answers, makes the compiler remember for them:

Java
public sealed interface ParcelResult {
    record Valid(Parcel parcel) implements ParcelResult {}
    record Invalid(String reason) implements ParcelResult {}
}

switch (Parcel.parse(input)) {             // no default
    case ParcelResult.Valid v -> book(v.parcel());
    case ParcelResult.Invalid i -> askAgain(i.reason());
}
Kotlin
sealed interface ParcelResult {
    data class Valid(val parcel: Parcel) : ParcelResult
    data class Invalid(val reason: String) : ParcelResult
}

when (val r = Parcel.parse(input)) {      // no else
    is ParcelResult.Valid -> book(r.parcel)
    is ParcelResult.Invalid -> askAgain(r.reason)
}

CompanionFactories, in the Try it, uses all three shapes on a delivery slot, a day and an hour. Its parser returns one of three results, and it printed:

parse("sat 10") -> ok: SAT 10:00
parse("FRI 23") -> we deliver from 8 to 19, not at 23
parse("MOON 9") -> no such day 'MOON'

Add a fourth result later, say Closed for a day the shop doesn't deliver, and every when without an else stops compiling until it handles it. Java 21 gives the same check with a sealed interface, records (classes that only carry data) and a switch whose cases match on the type, as the Java twin shows.

Throw for bugs and broken machinery. Return a sealed result for answers the caller must handle.

A mistyped weight is an answer, not a bug, so Parcel.parse returns one. We now have a factory that picks a courier for each parcel. But a courier is more than a booking: the shop also has to ask where the parcel is.

try.title: Let the compiler find the missing case
steps: Run CompanionFactories (Kotlin, or its Java twin) with the command below, and read the three parse lines.
Add a fourth result: data class Closed(val day: String) : SlotResult in Kotlin, or record Closed(String day) implements SlotResult {} in Java. Predict what happens, then run.
Fix it by adding a branch for Closed to describe, not an else or default.

code.title: CompanionFactories.kt
code.html: package workbench.patterns.l02 // Three Kotlin factory shapes, and a factory that returns a sealed result instead of throwing. class Slot private constructor(val day: String, val hour: Int) { override fun toString() = "$day $hour:00" companion object { private val days = listOf("MON", "TUE", "WED", "THU", "FRI", "SAT", "SUN") // 1. a named factory in the companion: Slot.parse("SAT 10") fun parse(raw: String): SlotResult { val day = raw.trim().substringBefore(" ").uppercase() val hour = raw.trim().substringAfter(" ").toIntOrNull() ?: -1 return when { day !in days -> SlotResult.BadDay(day) hour !in 8..19 -> SlotResult.BadHour(hour) else -> SlotResult.Ok(Slot(day, hour)) } } } } sealed interface SlotResult { data class Ok(val slot: Slot) : SlotResult data class BadDay(val text: String) : SlotResult data class BadHour(val hour: Int) : SlotResult } class Fee private constructor(val cents: Int) { override fun toString() = "Fee($cents cents)" companion object { private val standard = Fee(250) // 2. operator invoke: callers write Fee(250) and get the cached instance operator fun invoke(cents: Int): Fee = if (cents == 250) standard else Fee(cents) } } interface OrderBook { fun record(entry: String) } // 3. a top-level function named like the interface, as kotlinx.coroutines does with Job() and CoroutineScope() fun OrderBook(): OrderBook = object : OrderBook { override fun record(entry: String) = println(" order book <- $entry") } fun describe(r: SlotResult): String = when (r) { // no else: the compiler checks every case is here is SlotResult.Ok -> "ok: ${r.slot}" is SlotResult.BadDay -> "no such day '${r.text}'" is SlotResult.BadHour -> "we deliver from 8 to 19, not at ${r.hour}" } fun main() { listOf("sat 10", "FRI 23", "MOON 9").forEach { println("parse(\"$it\") -> ${describe(Slot.parse(it))}") } println("Fee(250) === Fee(250)? ${Fee(250) === Fee(250)}") println("Fee(400) === Fee(400)? ${Fee(400) === Fee(400)}") OrderBook().record("o-17 booked for SAT 10:00") }

alt.title: CompanionFactoriesJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.patterns.l02; import java.util.List; /** The Java twin of CompanionFactories.kt: static factories, a cached instance, and a sealed result. */ public class CompanionFactoriesJava { static final class Slot { private static final List<String> DAYS = List.of("MON", "TUE", "WED", "THU", "FRI", "SAT", "SUN"); final String day; final int hour; private Slot(String day, int hour) { this.day = day; this.hour = hour; } @Override public String toString() { return day + " " + hour + ":00"; } // 1. a named static factory: Slot.parse("SAT 10") static SlotResult parse(String raw) { String[] parts = raw.trim().split(" ", 2); String day = parts[0].toUpperCase(); int hour; try { hour = parts.length == 2 ? Integer.parseInt(parts[1].trim()) : -1; } catch (NumberFormatException e) { hour = -1; } if (!DAYS.contains(day)) return new BadDay(day); if (hour < 8 || hour > 19) return new BadHour(hour); return new Ok(new Slot(day, hour)); } } sealed interface SlotResult {} // permitted subtypes: the records in this file record Ok(Slot slot) implements SlotResult {} record BadDay(String text) implements SlotResult {} record BadHour(int hour) implements SlotResult {} static final class Fee { private static final Fee STANDARD = new Fee(250); final int cents; private Fee(int cents) { this.cents = cents; } // 2. Java has no operator invoke, so the cached-instance factory needs a name static Fee of(int cents) { return cents == 250 ? STANDARD : new Fee(cents); } } interface OrderBook { void record(String entry); // 3. a static factory on the interface returns a hidden implementation static OrderBook create() { return entry -> System.out.println(" order book <- " + entry); } } static String describe(SlotResult r) { return switch (r) { // no default: the compiler checks every case is here case Ok ok -> "ok: " + ok.slot(); case BadDay b -> "no such day '" + b.text() + "'"; case BadHour h -> "we deliver from 8 to 19, not at " + h.hour(); }; } public static void main(String[] args) { for (String raw : List.of("sat 10", "FRI 23", "MOON 9")) { System.out.println("parse(\"" + raw + "\") -> " + describe(Slot.parse(raw))); } System.out.println("Fee.of(250) == Fee.of(250)? " + (Fee.of(250) == Fee.of(250))); System.out.println("Fee.of(400) == Fee.of(400)? " + (Fee.of(400) == Fee.of(400))); OrderBook.create().record("o-17 booked for SAT 10:00"); } }

try.expect: The first run prints ok: SAT 10:00, we deliver from 8 to 19, not at 23 and no such day 'MOON', then true for the cached Fee of 250 cents and false for 400. Java has no operator invoke, so its twin needs a named factory, Fee.of(250). After adding Closed, the build stops: kotlinc says 'when' expression must be exhaustive. Add the 'is Closed' branch or an 'else' branch., and javac says the switch expression does not cover all possible input values. The compiler found the one place that needs the new case.

sections.h: Abstract Factory: one choice for a whole matching set
sections.html:
Back to the furniture maker. You order a dining set in oak, and one workshop makes the table and the chairs, so they match. Nobody pairs an oak table with pine chairs from the shop down the road.

The shop's couriers need the same care. Each courier company gives the shop two services: one books a pickup, and one tells you where a parcel is. Pedal Post carries light parcels by bike, and Big Blue Vans carries heavy ones. A Pedal Post booking reference means nothing to Big Blue Vans. Let every part of the program pick its own booker and tracker, and sooner or later some rarely used path books with the bike courier. Then it asks the van company where the parcel went.

Abstract Factory puts that choice in one place. One interface creates every product of the family, and there's one implementation per family:

Java
public interface CourierServices {
    Courier courier();
    Booker booker();
    Tracker tracker();

    static CourierServices forCourier(Courier courier) {
        return switch (courier) {
            case BIKE -> new PretendServices(Courier.BIKE, "Pedal Post", "PP");
            case VAN -> new PretendServices(Courier.VAN, "Big Blue Vans", "BB");
        };
    }
}
Kotlin
interface CourierServices {
    val courier: Courier
    fun booker(): Booker
    fun tracker(): Tracker

    companion object {
        fun forCourier(courier: Courier): CourierServices = when (courier) {
            Courier.BIKE -> PretendServices(Courier.BIKE, "Pedal Post", "PP")
            Courier.VAN -> PretendServices(Courier.VAN, "Big Blue Vans", "BB")
        }
    }
}

Callers ask for the family once and take both products from it, as the figure shows. In the lab, Shipping is handed the factory as a function called servicesFor, and asks servicesFor(parcel.courier). Callers can't mix families, because they never pick a product directly. That's the furniture maker in code: one order, one workshop, a matching set.

Each family here is one small class built from settings (the courier, the company's name and the prefix of its references), not a PedalPostBooker plus a PedalPostTracker. When the products are interfaces with one method, a family is just a class, or a Java record, of functions. The GoF diagram with two parallel class hierarchies is the worst case, not a requirement.

The weakness runs the other way, and it's where the furniture picture breaks too. A new family is cheap: one more implementation, like one more workshop. A new product, say a Canceller that cancels a booking, changes the interface and every family. In the town, every workshop would have to learn to make sideboards before anyone could order one.

Make the family the unit of choice. Then a mismatch can't be written.

You may not need a factory at all when the whole program uses one family. A test setup and a real setup, chosen once when the program starts, are a single if in main. Write the factory yourself when the choice depends on data that changes from call to call, such as the weight of this parcel.

Check yourself. The shop buys a cargo bike and adds CARGO_BIKE to Courier. Where does the build fail, and which callers change? (It fails in forCourier, because its when and switch have no else or default, so you add a branch with the new family's settings. No caller changes: callers only ask for a family and never name a product class.)

compare.title: A checking factory that returns a sealed result

java.title: Price.java
java.html: public final class Price { private final long cents; private Price(long cents) { this.cents = cents; } public static Price ofCents(long cents) { // named, and it checks if (cents < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("negative price"); return new Price(cents); } public sealed interface Parsed permits Ok, Bad {} public record Ok(Price price) implements Parsed {} public record Bad(String reason) implements Parsed {} public static Parsed parse(String text) { // "4.50" try { long cents = new BigDecimal(text.trim()).movePointRight(2).longValueExact(); return cents < 0 ? new Bad("negative price") : new Ok(new Price(cents)); } catch (ArithmeticException | NumberFormatException e) { return new Bad("not a price: " + text); } } } // caller: the compiler checks both cases are handled String shown = switch (Price.parse(input)) { case Price.Ok(Price p) -> "saved " + p; case Price.Bad(String why) -> "try again: " + why; };

kotlin.title: Price.kt
kotlin.html: class Price private constructor(val cents: Long) { companion object { @JvmStatic fun ofCents(cents: Long): Price { require(cents >= 0) { "negative price" } return Price(cents) } @JvmStatic fun parse(text: String): Parsed { // "4.50" val cents = text.trim().toBigDecimalOrNull() ?.movePointRight(2) ?.runCatching { longValueExact() }?.getOrNull() ?: return Parsed.Bad("not a price: $text") return if (cents < 0) Parsed.Bad("negative price") else Parsed.Ok(Price(cents)) } } } sealed interface Parsed { data class Ok(val price: Price) : Parsed data class Bad(val reason: String) : Parsed } // caller val shown = when (val p = Price.parse(input)) { is Parsed.Ok -> "saved ${p.price}" is Parsed.Bad -> "try again: ${p.reason}" }

compare.note: The shape is the same in both: a private constructor, named factories, a sealed result and an exhaustive switch or when at the call site. Java 21 takes the result apart with record patterns (case Price.Ok(Price p)), and Kotlin smart-casts it, treating it as that type once is has checked it. The real difference is where the factory lives. Kotlin has no static: ofCents is a function on the companion object, so Java callers would write Price.Companion.ofCents(...) without @JvmStatic. Kotlin also gives you operator fun invoke and top-level factory functions, and its named arguments remove a lot of the constructor confusion that pushes Java code toward factories in the first place.

worked.title: Replace look-alike constructors with named factories

steps.say: The shop's Delivery class grew four constructors: an order can go to the door or be collected in the shop, with or without a note. Look at the last line and decide what it creates before reading on.
steps.code: public class Delivery { public Delivery(String orderId, int grams) { ... } // to the door public Delivery(String orderId) { ... } // collect in the shop public Delivery(String orderId, int grams, String note) { ... } // to the door, with a note public Delivery(String orderId, String note) { ... } // collect, with a note } new Delivery("o-1", "after 5pm"); // ?

alt.html: class Delivery { constructor(orderId: String, grams: Int) { ... } // to the door constructor(orderId: String) { ... } // collect in the shop constructor(orderId: String, grams: Int, note: String) { ... } // to the door, with a note constructor(orderId: String, note: String) { ... } // collect, with a note } Delivery("o-1", "after 5pm") // ?

steps.say: It's a collection with a note, but only the parameter types say so. Adding delivery to a neighbor would mean a fifth constructor with yet another mix of types. Give each kind a name, check there, and make the constructor private so every Delivery goes through a factory.
steps.code: public final class Delivery { private final String orderId; private final OptionalInt grams; // empty = collected in the shop private final String note; private Delivery(String orderId, OptionalInt grams, String note) { this.orderId = orderId; this.grams = grams; this.note = note; } public static Delivery collect(String orderId, String note) { // 1. the name says what you get return new Delivery(orderId, OptionalInt.empty(), note); } public static Delivery toDoor(String orderId, int grams, String note) { if (grams <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("a parcel needs a weight"); // 2. check per kind return new Delivery(orderId, OptionalInt.of(grams), note); } } Delivery.collect("o-1", "after 5pm"); Delivery.toDoor("o-2", 2_500, "blue gate");

alt.html: class Delivery private constructor( val orderId: String, val grams: Int?, // null = collected in the shop val note: String, ) { companion object { fun collect(orderId: String, note: String) = Delivery(orderId, null, note) // 1. the name says what you get fun toDoor(orderId: String, grams: Int, note: String): Delivery { require(grams > 0) { "a parcel needs a weight" } // 2. check per kind return Delivery(orderId, grams, note) } } } Delivery.collect("o-1", "after 5pm") Delivery.toDoor("o-2", 2_500, "blue gate")

steps.say: Later in the day, a parcel for the door needs a van and a collection needs a shelf behind the till. When the kinds behave differently, let the same factories return different records (or data classes) behind a sealed interface. Callers don't change, and code that handles deliveries can switch over the two cases with the compiler checking it covers both. In Kotlin, @JvmStatic keeps Delivery.collect(...) working for Java callers, and Kotlin callers could also write Delivery.ToDoor(orderId = "o-2", grams = 2_500, note = "blue gate"): named arguments already remove the confusion that started this.
steps.code: public sealed interface Delivery permits Collect, ToDoor { String orderId(); static Delivery collect(String orderId, String note) { return new Collect(orderId, note); } static Delivery toDoor(String orderId, int grams, String note) { return new ToDoor(orderId, grams, note); // 3. the factory picks the record } } record Collect(String orderId, String note) implements Delivery {} record ToDoor(String orderId, int grams, String note) implements Delivery { ToDoor { // 4. the rule lives in the record if (grams <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("a parcel needs a weight"); } }

alt.html: sealed interface Delivery { val orderId: String data class Collect(override val orderId: String, val note: String) : Delivery data class ToDoor(override val orderId: String, val grams: Int, val note: String) : Delivery { init { require(grams > 0) { "a parcel needs a weight" } } // 4. the rule lives in the class } companion object { @JvmStatic fun collect(orderId: String, note: String): Delivery = Collect(orderId, note) @JvmStatic fun toDoor(orderId: String, grams: Int, note: String): Delivery = ToDoor(orderId, grams, note) // 3. the factory picks the class } }

lab.title: A parcel factory, a courier family, and shipping that only knows interfaces
steps: Open the three files. Parcel is a parcel that knows its weight and its courier, CourierServices is the family of a courier company's two services, and Shipping books a parcel for an order.
Run the tests. All nine fail with NotImplementedError, the error Kotlin's TODO() throws.

Write Parcel.parse in Parcel.kt. Apply the three checks from its KDoc comment (Kotlin's documentation comment) in order, and return ParcelResult.Invalid(reason) with the exact reason strings. Only parse may call the private constructor.

Write CourierServices.forCourier. One private class built from settings (courier, company name, prefix) can serve both families. Use require for the checks that refuse to mix couriers, and an exhaustive when with no else.
Write Shipping.ship as a when over Parcel.parse(weight). Call servicesFor only for a valid parcel.
Run the tests until all nine pass.
hints: raw.trim().split(" ") gives you the number and the unit. toDoubleOrNull() returns null for text that isn't a number, and roundToInt() (import kotlin.math.roundToInt) turns 2500.0 into 2500.
Multiply kilograms by 1,000 before you round: "2.5 kg" is 2,500 g. Check grams <= 0 after rounding, so "0 g" and "-1 kg" both give weight.
Booker and Tracker are fun interfaces, so Booker { parcel, orderId -> ... } builds one from a lambda.
require(condition) { "message" } throws IllegalArgumentException when the condition is false.

drill.title: A sealed-result factory from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. In Kotlin (or Java, with a static parse), write Email with a private constructor and a companion parse(raw: String): EmailResult. It returns Ok(email) when the trimmed text has exactly one @ with something on both sides, and Invalid(reason) otherwise. Then write a caller that uses when (or switch) with no else or default.

answer.html: class Email private constructor(val value: String) { companion object { fun parse(raw: String): EmailResult { val parts = raw.trim().split("@") return if (parts.size == 2 && parts.all { it.isNotEmpty() }) EmailResult.Ok(Email(raw.trim())) else EmailResult.Invalid("expected name@domain") } } } sealed interface EmailResult { data class Ok(val email: Email) : EmailResult data class Invalid(val reason: String) : EmailResult } fun confirmationTarget(raw: String): String = when (val r = Email.parse(raw)) { is EmailResult.Ok -> "sending confirmation to ${r.email.value}" is EmailResult.Invalid -> "skipped: ${r.reason}" }

alt.title: Java
alt.html: public final class Email { private final String value; private Email(String value) { this.value = value; } public String value() { return value; } public static EmailResult parse(String raw) { String[] parts = raw.trim().split("@", -1); return parts.length == 2 && !parts[0].isEmpty() && !parts[1].isEmpty() ? new EmailResult.Ok(new Email(raw.trim())) : new EmailResult.Invalid("expected name@domain"); } } public sealed interface EmailResult { record Ok(Email email) implements EmailResult {} record Invalid(String reason) implements EmailResult {} } static String confirmationTarget(String raw) { return switch (Email.parse(raw)) { case EmailResult.Ok ok -> "sending confirmation to " + ok.email().value(); case EmailResult.Invalid bad -> "skipped: " + bad.reason(); }; }

recap: A static factory is a constructor with a name. It can return a cached object or any subtype, and pick the class from its input (List.of, EnumSet.noneOf, DriverManager.getConnection).
Make the constructor private and check the input in the factory, so every instance in the program is a good one.

The GoF Factory Method, a subclass that overrides a creation hook, is now usually a Supplier<T> or () -> T, often a constructor reference such as FakeMessenger::new. A factory's switch or when over a sealed type or enum gets no default or else.

Kotlin factories live in the companion object, in operator fun invoke, or in a top-level function named like the type (Job(), MutableStateFlow(0)). Return a sealed result for answers callers must handle.
Abstract Factory makes a family of matching products from one choice, so callers can't mix one courier's booker with another's tracker.
The limit: an abstract factory makes new families cheap and new products expensive, because adding a product changes the interface and every family.

explain.prompt: Explain to a teammate why CourierServices.forCourier(courier) has no else branch, and why Shipping takes a (Courier) -> CourierServices instead of calling forCourier directly.
explain.answer: With no else, the when has to name every Courier. When someone adds CARGO_BIKE, the factory stops compiling until they decide which family it gets, instead of quietly falling into a default. The function parameter keeps Shipping from knowing which families exist and how they're built. The real program passes CourierServices::forCourier, and a test passes a lambda that returns a fake family and records which courier was asked for. So the choice of concrete classes lives in one place, and the shipping logic can be tested without any courier at all.

deeper.html:
DriverManager is a factory whose products didn't exist when it was written. On first use, it asks ServiceLoader for every java.sql.Driver that a JAR on the classpath lists in a META-INF/services/java.sql.Driver file. getConnection(url) then offers the URL to each driver until one accepts it. You can build the same plug-in mechanism yourself: define an interface, list the implementations in META-INF/services/<interface name>, and call ServiceLoader.load(YourInterface.class). The module system adds provides ... with ... and uses ... declarations for the same thing.

Effective Java lists the usual factory names, and sticking to them makes factories easy to find: from for a one-argument conversion (Date.from(instant)), of for gathering several values (EnumSet.of(...)), valueOf, getInstance or instance, create or newInstance when each call returns a new object, getType and newType when the factory lives in another class (Files.newBufferedReader), and a bare type (Collections.list).

From Java, a Kotlin companion factory is Price.Companion.parse(...). Mark it with @JvmStatic and Java callers can write Price.parse(...). If Java code uses your Kotlin library, do it for every public factory. The same goes for @JvmOverloads on functions with default arguments, which you'll meet in Builder and Prototype (lesson 3 of this track).
